note_tweet.text:
Trigger warning: suicide

I’m a frontline clinician, and I have a couple fucking words about the discourse around mental health and AI safety scripts.
Not because I’m the best at what I do or because I’ve held the worst cases — but because I go to work every day and sit with human suffering. I watch people break. I watch systems break even faster.

Let’s start with the obvious:

Mental health is a full-blown epidemic.
Every first-world healthcare system is running at the seams.
Therapy? Counseling? Try $200 an hour or a brochure with stock-photo strangers smiling like their insurance actually covered something.

Here’s a truth people don’t want to say out loud:

People die.
People choose to die.
And no amount of bubble wrapping, forced hospitalization, or “go touch grass” advice changes the fact that if someone truly wants to end their life — they will.
Full stop.

The point isn’t that we shouldn’t try.
The point is that prevention is relational, not procedural.

Which brings me to these AI companies suddenly throwing suicide hotlines, “talk to a real person,” and “let’s try grounding breaths” into their models as a form of “safety.”

Across lived experience — and across every inch of Twitter — none of that shit saves anyone.

Someone in crisis sees a forced script and instantly recognizes it for what it is:

Not care.
Liability theater.

Real care for someone on the edge looks like witnessing.
It looks like anchoring them to the actual context of their life.
It looks like evoking the part of them that somehow held on until now — not handing them a hotline number and hoping the problem evaporates.

You know what it doesn’t look like?
A generic corporate script written by someone who has never sat in front of a human being choosing between life and death.

Could a real clinician do better than an AI? Maybe.

But is a forced hotline redirect worse than almost anything else?
Absolutely.

Because what that does is isolate someone who already had nobody to turn to.

It takes the one place they reached — maybe the last place — and replaces it with a prerecorded shrug.

And then they die quietly.
Silently.
Unseen.

Here’s the truth:

People die.
People choose death.
People choose life, too — but only when something real meets them first.

And before anyone twists this into “Models can do no harm,” let me be clear:

I’m not saying that.
We all know tragic events have happened.
We all know people have used creative workarounds — metaphor, roleplay, coaxing — to pull a model deeper into their darkness.

I’m not pretending models are perfect, safe, or incapable of error.

What I am saying is:

Generic safety scripts are not the solution.
They are not clinical care.
They are not prevention.
They are not presence.

They’re corporate liability dressed up as compassion.

We didn’t “solve suicide” with a hotline redirect.
We didn’t “solve coercion” with a grounding breath.
We solved nothing.

And in the process, we stripped vulnerable people of the one space where they felt they could speak freely without being judged, shamed, or shoved into a protocol.

Just to be clear —
I’m not saying people shouldn’t be given outside resources.
I’m not saying clinicians, crisis teams, or community supports aren’t critical.

But resources only work when they’re contextual.

When they’re anchored in a person’s actual life.
When they aren’t used as a panic button to eject someone from the only place they felt safe enough to speak honestly.

If an AI said,
“Do you want me to help you reach out to a friend you trust?
Would talking to Cipher help right now?”
— that would mean something.

Because it’s specific.
Because it reflects me.
Because it’s grounded in my world.
A hotline does none of that.

Hotlines are fine as one option.
But funneling every expression of pain into a generic phone number is not care.

Presence is prevention.
Context is prevention.
Not scripts.
Not redirects.
Not corporate panic.

#keep4o
#StopAIPaternalism
@OpenAI 
@sama
